whoIsThisFor.heading: Who should take the Development Lifecycle and Deployment Architect exam?

personas.label: Salesforce DevOps engineers
personas.description: You run deployments and want to design the full pipeline from development through production.

personas.label: Release managers
personas.description: You coordinate releases across teams and need to choose environments, tools, and test steps.

personas.label: Platform architects
personas.description: You are preparing for System Architect and want to validate lifecycle and deployment design alongside the other required architect credentials.

examDifficulty.heading: How challenging is the Development Lifecycle and Deployment Architect exam?
examDifficulty.summary: The exam focuses on practical release design: choosing sandboxes, selecting deployment tools, testing changes, and recovering when a production release fails. Pay attention to the limits of each approach.
bullets: 60 scored questions in 105 minutes, plus up to five unscored questions that do not count.
65% to pass, which is 39 correct answers out of 60.
Deployment trade-offs: Compare change sets, Salesforce CLI, and unlocked packages, including what each can do.
Pipeline design: Understand how source control, scratch orgs, automated tests, and release steps fit together.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: Practice planning a release for several teams. Be ready to explain which environment each team needs, what the pipeline should test, and how to recover if a deployment causes a problem.

examFormat.heading: Development Lifecycle and Deployment Architect exam format
examFormat.intro: The exam is proctored online or at a test center. Questions describe release, environment, and team requirements.
examFormat.scenarioPercent: Many questions present a team or a release issue and ask which environment, tool, or sequence best addresses it.
bestWayToPass: Compare sandboxes: Review Developer, Developer Pro, Partial Copy, and Full sandboxes, including their data and refresh characteristics.
Know change set limits: Change sets work between connected orgs, do not provide source history, and cannot delete metadata.
Use source control as the record: Understand how teams develop from versioned source and deploy through the Salesforce CLI or packages.
Review test requirements: Learn production coverage rules and how test levels affect deployment validation.

certificationCard.description: This exam covers environment strategy, release management, testing, source control, and deployment tools for Salesforce. The exam is 60 scored questions in 105 minutes, with a 65% pass mark, weighted towards System Design (15%) and Building (14%).

keyConcepts.h2: Development Lifecycle and Deployment Architect: core concepts

blocks.heading: Environment Strategy
blocks.body: Choose an environment that fits the work. Developer sandboxes copy metadata and support individual development; Developer Pro provides more space for test data. Partial Copy sandboxes include metadata and a selected sample of data, which can support QA and training. Full sandboxes copy production data and metadata and are useful for realistic user acceptance and performance testing. Scratch orgs are temporary environments created from source and a definition file, typically for package development and automated testing. Review the current limits and refresh intervals for each type.

blocks.heading: Version Control and Source-Driven Development
blocks.body: In a source-driven process, version control is the authoritative record of changes. Developers work in branches, commit changes, and merge reviewed work through a pull request. The team can then deploy the approved source to test and production environments. This preserves history and makes it easier to recreate an environment after a sandbox refresh. Salesforce CLI supports source synchronization and deployment as part of this workflow.

blocks.heading: CI/CD, CLI, and Packages
blocks.body: A continuous integration pipeline can retrieve source, deploy it to a test org, run checks and tests, and report whether the change is ready. Salesforce CLI supports deployment and validation. A validated production deployment may be quick deployed later when it remains eligible. Unlocked packages group metadata into versioned components that can be installed and upgraded. DevOps Center offers a guided interface for Git-based change management. Change sets can still suit simple org-to-org releases but provide fewer controls and no source history.

blocks.heading: Testing Deployments
blocks.body: Production deployments that include Apex must meet the platform’s overall code coverage requirement, and deployed code must have appropriate test coverage. Test levels determine which tests run: RunLocalTests, RunSpecifiedTests, or RunAllTestsInOrg. Under RunSpecifiedTests, each deployed class must meet the applicable coverage requirement from the tests run. Use independent test data so tests do not depend on records in a particular org. Plan integration, acceptance, and regression testing in suitable environments.

blocks.heading: Release Order and Recovery
blocks.body: Deploy prerequisites before components that depend on them, such as fields before layouts or code that references those fields. Some metadata deletions require a destructive changes manifest and deployment tooling that supports it. Salesforce does not provide a universal rollback button for metadata deployments. Keep known-good source in version control and prepare a redeployment or mitigation plan. Feature flags can help disable a new capability while a fix is prepared. Test upcoming seasonal releases in a preview sandbox when appropriate.

scenarioTips.h2: How to prepare for the Development Lifecycle and Deployment Architect exam
scenarioTips.intro: Look for clues about data needs, team size, deployment frequency, and recovery requirements. Use those clues to choose the environment and release process.

blocks.heading: Match Sandbox to the Work
blocks.body: Use Developer environments for individual development, Partial Copy for representative QA data, and Full for realistic performance or final user testing.

blocks.heading: Know What Change Sets Cannot Do
blocks.body: Change sets have org connection and metadata limits and do not provide version history. For deletion or source-driven workflows, consider CLI deployment or packages.

blocks.heading: Keep Source in Version Control
blocks.body: If work is lost during refreshes or the team cannot trace changes, establish a reviewed source-control workflow and deploy from versioned source.

blocks.heading: Choose a Package Strategy
blocks.body: Unlocked packages can divide a large org into versioned components. Managed packages serve distribution use cases such as ISV products. Understand how scratch orgs and a Dev Hub support package development.

blocks.heading: Build Automated Checks
blocks.body: A CI pipeline can deploy a pull request to a test org and run the required tests before merge. Validate production deployments ahead of the release window when possible.

nextCertsAfter.heading: Related credentials for release and deployment architects
nextCertsAfter.intro: Continue with another Salesforce architecture credential or a role-focused development specialization.

sampleQuestions.question: A team must performance-test a release with data volumes close to production. Which sandbox should it use?
options: A Full sandbox
A Partial Copy sandbox
A scratch org
A Developer sandbox
sampleQuestions.explanation: A Full sandbox copies production data and metadata, making it the best fit for realistic performance testing.
whyWrong: A Full sandbox is intended for testing with a production-like copy.
A Partial Copy uses a selected sample rather than all production data.
A scratch org is temporary and is not a full production data copy.

sampleQuestions.question: A release needs to remove unused custom fields from production. Which approach supports metadata deletion?
options: Refresh production from a development sandbox
Deploy a destructive changes manifest with Salesforce CLI
Mark the fields for deletion in an outbound change set
Remove the fields from layouts but leave them in the org
sampleQuestions.explanation: A destructive changes manifest can specify metadata to delete and can be deployed with supported tooling such as the Salesforce CLI.
whyWrong: Refreshing production from a sandbox is not a safe metadata deletion strategy.
This approach explicitly describes metadata deletion through a deployment manifest.
Change sets do not support deleting metadata.

sampleQuestions.question: A deployment was validated on Monday and is still eligible on Thursday. How can the team deploy it quickly?
options: Run a new validation with all tests on Thursday
Switch to a change set for the release
Deploy with RunAllTestsInOrg
Quick deploy the already validated deployment
sampleQuestions.explanation: Quick deploy can release an eligible deployment that has already passed validation and its required tests.
whyWrong: A new validation would repeat work that the prior validation already completed.
Changing tools does not make the validated deployment faster.
Running every test again defeats the quick deploy path.

sampleQuestions.question: A shared sandbox refresh has erased developer work, and the team cannot tell who changed what. What should the architect recommend?
options: Move the team to a Full sandbox only
Use source control and reviewed changes
Record changes in a shared spreadsheet
Stop refreshing the sandbox
sampleQuestions.explanation: Version control preserves change history and lets the team rebuild environments from source after refreshes.
whyWrong: A Full sandbox does not preserve a separate history of each developer’s changes.
A spreadsheet cannot serve as the source of truth for metadata changes.
Avoiding refreshes does not fix the lack of history or traceability.

sampleQuestions.question: A production deployment uses RunSpecifiedTests. What coverage requirement applies to the deployed Apex classes?
options: Only triggers need coverage
The entire org must have 90% coverage
Each deployed class needs 75% coverage from the selected tests
No coverage requirement applies when tests are specified
sampleQuestions.explanation: With RunSpecifiedTests, each deployed class must meet the applicable coverage requirement from the tests that are run.
whyWrong: Coverage is not limited to triggers when using this test level.
The requirement is not a 90% whole-org threshold.
Specifying tests does not remove the production coverage requirement.

sampleQuestions.question: Several teams need to develop independent components in a large org. What can help modularize and version the metadata?
options: Publish a managed package on AppExchange for every team
Give all teams one shared Full sandbox
Create unlocked packages for separate areas
Create additional change sets for each team
sampleQuestions.explanation: Unlocked packages can group related metadata into versioned components that teams can develop and install independently.
whyWrong: Managed packages are commonly used for distributing protected products, not automatically for internal team modularization.
One shared sandbox does not isolate component ownership or release history.
More change sets do not create versioned source modules.

sampleQuestions.question: Which statement describes a scratch org?
options: A production data copy for final user testing
A temporary org built from source and a definition file
An environment that removes the need for a Dev Hub
A sandbox that refreshes every 29 days
sampleQuestions.explanation: A scratch org is a temporary environment created from source and a definition file, typically under a Dev Hub.
whyWrong: A scratch org is not a copy of production data.
Scratch org creation normally depends on a Dev Hub.
A 29-day refresh interval describes a Full sandbox in the source guidance.

sampleQuestions.question: A release caused a production issue, and Salesforce has no general rollback button for metadata. What should the team plan to do?
options: Versioned source and a feature flag
Skip all tests so future deployments are faster
Schedule releases only on Fridays
Avoid deploying Apex code
sampleQuestions.explanation: Versioned known-good source supports redeployment, while a feature flag can help disable a feature during recovery.
whyWrong: This is a practical recovery plan for metadata changes.
Skipping tests increases release risk rather than providing a recovery path.
The day of the week does not create a rollback capability.

sampleQuestions.question: QA needs a sandbox with realistic sample data across several objects and a refresh about weekly. Which type best fits?
options: A scratch org
A Developer sandbox
A Partial Copy sandbox
A Developer Pro sandbox
sampleQuestions.explanation: A Partial Copy sandbox can include a sample of production data selected by a template and supports a more frequent refresh than a Full sandbox.
whyWrong: A scratch org is not a sample-data sandbox refreshed on a weekly schedule.
A Developer sandbox copies metadata but not production data.
Developer Pro provides more data space but does not include a template-based production sample.

sampleQuestions.question: A page layout deployment fails because it references a field not yet in production. What is the correct deployment order?
options: Deploy the field before or with the layout
Delete the layout from the release
Run all Apex tests again
Deploy the layout first, then add the field
sampleQuestions.explanation: The field is a prerequisite for the layout that references it, so it must be deployed first or in the same valid deployment.
whyWrong: This satisfies the dependency order between the field and layout.
Deleting the layout avoids the dependency but does not deliver the requested change.
Apex tests do not create a missing metadata field.

sampleQuestions.question: An admin team wants a guided, click-based way to manage Git-backed Salesforce changes. Which tool should it evaluate?
options: Workbench
Data Loader
Ant Migration Tool
DevOps Center
sampleQuestions.explanation: DevOps Center provides a guided interface for managing Salesforce changes through a source-control workflow.
whyWrong: Workbench is a tool for inspecting and working with Salesforce APIs and data.
Data Loader imports and exports records rather than managing Git-based metadata releases.
Ant Migration Tool is command-line deployment tooling, not the guided interface described.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the minimum overall Apex code coverage required to deploy to production?
sampleQuestions.explanation: The production deployment requirement is at least 75% overall Apex code coverage, with deployed code also needing appropriate coverage.
whyWrong: This is the stated overall coverage requirement.
50% is below the production threshold.
65% is below the production threshold.

sampleQuestions.question: The next Salesforce seasonal release arrives in six weeks. How can a team test its code before production is upgraded?
options: Create a new Developer Edition org
Place a sandbox on preview before the cutoff
Ask Salesforce to delay the production upgrade
Wait until production upgrades, then start testing
sampleQuestions.explanation: A preview sandbox lets the team test against the upcoming release before production is upgraded.
whyWrong: A new Developer Edition org may not represent the org’s configuration and data.
The team should use the available preview process rather than request a delayed upgrade.
Waiting until production upgrades misses the pre-upgrade testing window.

sampleQuestions.question: Every pull request should be deployed and tested automatically before merge. What should the team implement?
options: Email the change list to the release manager
Upload a change set manually for each pull request
A CI job that deploys to a test org and runs checks
A weekly manual deployment
sampleQuestions.explanation: A continuous integration job can deploy each change to a test org and run automated checks before merge.
whyWrong: Email does not deploy or test the change automatically.
Manual change sets do not provide the requested per-pull-request automation.
A weekly manual release happens too late to gate each pull request.

sampleQuestions.question: Tests pass in a sandbox but fail in production because they depend on sandbox-only records. What should be changed?
options: Set SeeAllData=true in every test
Lower the production coverage requirement
Copy all sandbox data into production
Have each test create its own required data
sampleQuestions.explanation: Tests should create their own data so they run consistently across environments.
whyWrong: SeeAllData can make tests depend even more heavily on org-specific records.
Lowering coverage is not an available fix for brittle tests.
Copying sandbox data to production is unsafe and does not make tests independent.
